newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Exxon goes aheads with big Singapore plant.
newsitem.headline: Exxon goes aheads with big Singapore plant.

text.p: Exxon Chemical Co, a division of Exxon Corp, said on Friday it had decided to go ahead with plans to build a US$2.0 billion petrochemical complex in Singapore.
It said in a statement the complex centred around a steam cracker that will produce 800,000 tonnes of ethylene a year. It is due to start operations in 2000.
The plant will be integrated with Esso Singapore's existing 230,000-barrel-per-day refinery at the same site on Pulau Ayer Chawan, an island off Singapore.

"The worldscale size of the plants, coupled with the strong advantage of being integrated with a major Exxon refinery, will enable the...(plant) to supply highly competitive products to the region's growing markets," Warwick Bisley, managing director of the new venture, told a news conference.
Exxon said J.W. Kellogg and Japan's Chiyoda Corp would build the main cracker that will also produce 400,000 tonnes of propylene and 200,000 tonnes of butadiene a year.
The company said it would also build three downstream plants with annual capacities of 450,000 tonnes of polyethylene, 275,000 tonnes of polypropylene and 150,000 tonnes of oxo-alcohol.
The statement said construction contracts for the downstream plants would be awarded later.
These downstream plants will consume about 60 percent of the output from the steam cracker.
Exxon is currently negotiating with two or three other companies that already have plans to build plants at the site to take the remaining output.
"We do not plan to export the olefins (ethylene, propylene) produced," Bisley said.
He said the company was in an advanced stage of negotiations with these companies to secure an offtake agreement but declined to identity them.
Polyethylene and polypropylene are basic plastics while oxo-alcohol is used to make plasticizers that are used for the production of wire and cable insulation and floor coverings.

Bisley said he was confident of the sucess of the new complex despite industry talk of an over supply in 2000 as several other plants are due to start elsewhere in Southeast Asia at much the same time.
"Our assessment is that there is room in the market for this capacity," he said. "We must make sure that we have the lowest cost in the region."
